stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Judengasse, house of origin
stops.campa: Into the tight lane of the Frankfurt Judengasse, walled and gated at both ends, a son is born on 21 June to the Oppenheimer line, merchants and bankers expelled once already from this city in 1612 and scattered through the Rhineland. The family is threaded across half the courts of the Reich: a brother will lead the Jews of Heidelberg and Fürth, a nephew will become the great rabbi-collector of Prague. The boy is raised inside the great commercial network of Ashkenaz, where credit travels faster than any horse.

stops.name: Heidelberg, purveyor to Elector Karl Ludwig
stops.campa: Under the ruined-and-rebuilt castle on the Neckar, Samuel takes up service to Karl Ludwig, Elector Palatine, in a land bled white by the Thirty Years' War. He becomes purveyor to the elector and tax-collector of Palatine Jewry: the man who feeds an army and gathers a community's dues in the same ledger. Here he learns his craft: to advance grain, horses and coin against a prince's promise, and to make a prince's need his own security. The risky transactions begin that will one day carry him to the Kaiser's own table.

stops.name: Mannheim, the widening consortium
stops.campa: Across the Palatinate, in Mannheim, in Worms, along the Rhine trade, Samuel weaves a web of partners and agents, Jewish and Christian both, who move money and provisions between the fairs of Frankfurt and the magazines of the frontier. He is no longer a single supplier but the hub of a network. When the great war between the Kaiser and Louis XIV opens in 1673, an Austrian general marching on the Rhine notices the man who can furnish an army where the crown's own commissaries fail.

stops.name: The Rhine front, supplier to the imperial army against France
stops.campa: The Dutch War draws the Kaiser west against Louis XIV, and along the Rhine, through Worms and the Palatine towns, Samuel assembles a consortium to victual the Austrian army in the field. This is his proving ground on the imperial stage: not a single elector's household now but the Habsburg host itself learns to depend on his wagons of grain and his advances of silver. The general who watches him work will carry his name to Vienna, and the recommendation that opens the sealed city.

stops.name: Vienna, permitted through the closed gate
stops.campa: Four years after the Kaiser drove every Jew out of Vienna and razed their quarter in the Unterer Werd, the gate opens for one man. Samuel Oppenheimer is granted entry to the forbidden city and the right to bring his Gesinde, his household and a company of Jewish families, behind him. He works, from the first, for one master alone: Leopold I. He is the exception that the emptied city cannot do without, the single Jew the crown cannot afford to expel, because the crown cannot afford its own wars.

stops.name: Vienna, appointed Imperial War Factor
stops.campa: On the recommendation of Margrave Ludwig of Baden, the imperial general in Hungary, to whom Samuel has advanced 100,000 gulden for the war, Leopold names him Oberfaktor and court Jew, and by 1679 imperial war factor outright. The title makes him the emperor's supplier: uniforms and bread, muskets and powder, horses for the cavalry and fodder for the horses, pay for the troops and hospitals for the wounded. By 1682 the entire commissariat of the Habsburg armies runs through his ledgers.

stops.name: Vienna, the palace on the Bauernmarkt
stops.campa: He receives what no Jew has held here in living memory: leave to build a great house in the heart of the city, at the Bauernmarkt near the Bäckerstrasse, across from a tavern. From its rooms his agents ride to every frontier; into its cellars flow the contracts and receipts of an empire's war. The mansion is the visible sign of an invisible power: the credit of one household propping up the crown of the Caesars. It is also, one day, a target.

stops.name: Vienna, the Turkish host at the walls
stops.campa: In mid-July the army of the Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa, near two hundred thousand strong, closes upon Vienna and begins to dig. The emperor and his court flee up the Danube to Passau. The city is sealed, mined beneath its bastions, starving. And yet the contract Samuel signed does not lapse when the master runs: he stands to his bargain. Through the tightening ring and beyond it, his agents keep the magazines filling for the army that must be raised to break the siege.

stops.name: The relief army, provisioning the Entsatzheer
stops.campa: Above the besieged city the deliverance is assembled: the imperial army under Charles of Lorraine, the Poles under King Jan Sobieski, the men of the German electors. An army cannot march on courage alone. Samuel Oppenheimer takes upon himself the supply of the whole relieving host: bread and powder, remounts and fodder, coin for the soldiers, the logistics of salvation. The Court Jew, forbidden the city eleven years before, now victuals the sword that will save Christendom's gate.

stops.name: The Kahlenberg, the charge that breaks the host
stops.campa: On 12 September the Christian army pours down the wooded slopes of the Kahlenberg above the Danube. In the late afternoon Sobieski leads the greatest cavalry charge the age has seen; the Ottoman line shatters, Kara Mustafa flees, and the siege is broken in a single day. The city is saved. Fed and armed by Samuel's contracts, the deliverance holds, and the Jew who could not enter Vienna has helped to keep it. Even so, this very year he and his son are briefly seized, then freed: the crown's need protects him.

stops.name: Ofen (Buda), the Danube fleet of rafts
stops.campa: The war turns from defence to conquest, driving the Ottoman back down the Danube. For the siege of Ofen, Buda, the old Hungarian crown-city held by the Turk for a century and a half, Samuel builds a whole fleet of rafts to float provisions down the river to the besiegers. On 2 September the fortress falls. Behind every imperial magazine on the Hungarian plain stands the Oberfaktor's signature; the reconquest of a kingdom rides on his credit.

stops.name: Philippsburg, the son taken as surety
stops.campa: War flares again on the Rhine as Louis XIV strikes east. To force faster deliveries to the imperial army at Philippsburg, the court seizes Samuel's son Emanuel and holds him as a pledge: hostage against a merchant's speed. It is the pattern of his whole life laid bare: the crown leans on him utterly, and answers his indispensability with the mailed fist. He keeps the wagons rolling; the son is loosed. The debt, meanwhile, climbs without pause.
